en: Peṭakopadesa 2.
The Second Plane: The Foundation of the Dispensation.
Therein, what is the foundation of the Dispensation?
The discourse dealing with defilement, the discourse dealing with purification, the discourse dealing with penetration, the discourse dealing with the one beyond training;
the discourse dealing with both defilement and purification; the discourse dealing with both defilement and penetration;
the discourse dealing with both defilement, penetration, and the one beyond training; and the discourse dealing with both purification and penetration.
Instruction, fruit, means; instruction and fruit; fruit and means; instruction, fruit, and means.
Gratification, danger, escape; gratification and danger; gratification and escape; danger and escape; gratification, danger, and escape.
Mundane, supramundane, mundane and supramundane.
Kamma, vipāka, and both kamma and vipāka;
the indicated, the unindicated, and both the indicated and the unindicated;
knowledge, the object of knowledge, and both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Vision, cultivation, and both vision and cultivation.
Resultant kamma, non-resultant kamma, and neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant kamma.
One’s own statement, another’s statement, and both one’s own statement and another’s statement.
The formulation in terms of beings, the formulation in terms of phenomena, both the formulation in terms of beings and the formulation in terms of phenomena.

Praise, the formulation in terms of one’s own words, the formulation in terms of the words of others, both the formulation in terms of one’s own words and the formulation in terms of the words of others.
Action, result, both action and result.
Permitted, prohibited, and both permitted and prohibited—
these are the six types of prohibitions.
In this context, what is a discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*)?
Enveloped by the net of craving, covered by the veil of thirst,
they are bound by their kinsman, the heedless one.
Like fish at the mouth of a fishing net,
they pursue aging and death,
just as a suckling calf follows its mother.
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances.
In this regard, what is the discourse dealing with the residual impression?
‘Phenomena are preceded by the mind.’”
Mind is supreme, mind-made;
if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, [happiness follows].
Then happiness follows him,
never leaving him, like a shadow that never departs.
This is a sutta from the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

To Mahānāma the Sakyan, in the city of Kapilavatthu among the Sakyans, the Blessed One spoke this discourse, which is refined by policy in detail and refined by the cultivation of faith and virtue; that indeed was at the final time.
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*)?
"Above, below, and everywhere, completely liberated..."
Not contemplating "I am this," thus liberated, he has crossed over the flood,
which was never crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming.
“Are the precepts indeed for some purpose? Ānanda asks the Teacher.
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to the one beyond training (*asekkha*)?
“He whose mind is like a rock...”
It does not waver from what is established;
detached from things that cause passion,
it is not provoked by things that cause anger.
“For one whose mind is thus developed,
from where will suffering come?”— this is the Elder Sāriputta,
a certain disciple of the Blessed One, who, having insulted me and not relinquishing his position, has departed on his journey; an explanation regarding Sāriputta must be made.
"For whomsoever, indeed, the Blessed One has not developed and cultivated mindfulness directed to the body in detail... [as should be done].
In that regard, what is that which pertains to defilement and that which pertains to purification?
"The rain pours down upon one who covers."
The open does not rain upon;
therefore, uncover what is covered,
so that it may not rain upon you.
"He rains upon the covered" refers to defilement (*saṅkileso*).
"He does not rain upon the uncovered" refers to latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
"Darkness with darkness as its destination" is explained in detail.
In this context, that which is darkness and that which is destined for darkness is defilement (*saṅkileso*).
That which is light and that which is destined for light is purification (*vāsanā*).
In this regard, what is the discourse pertaining both to defilement and to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*)?
The wise do not call that a strong bond which is made of iron,
wood, or rope; rather, they call it a strong bond to be infatuated with and enamored of jewels and earrings.
"The longing for children and wives—the wise do not call that a strong bond; rather, when there is longing for children and wives, this is defilement.
Having cut even this, the wise go forth, free from longing and having abandoned all sensual desires—this is penetration.
That which is willed and that which is intended, and the descent of name-and-form—
by these four terms there is defilement;
by the latter four, penetration.
In this regard, what is the discourse that pertains to defilement, to penetration, and to the state of one beyond training?
"This world is born of anguish;
overcome by contact, it calls disease 'self'."
For in whatever way they conceive it,
that thing becomes otherwise.
The world, attached to existence, is subject to change.
One who is bound to existence delights only in existence;
what one delights in is fear,
and that from which one fears is suffering.
Moreover, this holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning existence.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins have claimed liberation from existence by means of further existence, I declare them all to be "unliberated from existence.
And whatever ascetics or brahmins have claimed escape from existence by means of non-existence, I declare them all to be "not escaped from existence."

For it is dependent on acquisitions (*upadhi*) that this suffering arises; with the destruction of all clinging (*upādāna*), there is no arising of suffering. Behold this world: beings are overcome by manifold ignorance, delighting in what has come to be, not yet liberated from becoming.
Whatever states of existence there may be—everywhere and in every respect—all those states of existence are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
"Thus is this, according to reality."
For one who sees with right wisdom,
craving for existence is abandoned,
and one does not delight in non-existence.
With the total destruction of craving,
there is the remainderless fading away and cessation that is Nibbāna.
For that bhikkhu who has attained extinction—
Without clinging, there is no further becoming;
Māra is overcome, the battle is won,
and such a one has transcended all states of existence.
“This world is born of anguish, even unto suffering”—this refers to the defilement of craving.

Furthermore, regarding those re-grasping [at existence], whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared liberation from existence through further existence, I say they are all “unliberated from existence.
Or again, whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared escape from existence through non-existence, I say they are “not escaped from existence.”
This is the corruption of views; that corruption of views and the corruption of craving—both together constitute corruption.
Furthermore, the holy life lived for the sake of abandoning existence, leading as far as the total destruction of clinging and the cessation of becoming, is the portion pertaining to penetration.
For that extinguished bhikkhu, the passage from "he has transcended all states of being, such a one" constitutes the portion pertaining to the one beyond training (asekkha).
There are four types of persons: one who goes with the stream is defilement; one who stands firm is the state of being established; and one who goes against the stream is penetration.
"He stands on dry land" refers to the stage of one beyond training (*asekkha*).
In this context, what is the discourse pertaining to both spiritual cultivation (*vāsanā*) and penetration (*nibbedha*)?
“Merit increases for one who gives;
enmity does not accumulate for one who is self-restrained;
and the skillful person abandons evil.”
“Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is fully quenched”—this is the habituation.
“Merit increases for the giver; enmity is not accumulated by the self-controlled”—this is the habituation.
“The skillful one abandons evil; through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is fully quenched”—this is penetration.
When teachings have been entered through the ear, mastered by speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view, five benefits are to be expected.

Here, someone has many teachings that are learned, retained, not forgotten, mastered by speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view. By applying himself, striving, and exerting effort, he attains distinction in this very life.
If he does not attain distinction in this very life, he attains it when he is sick.
If he does not attain it while ill, he attains it at the time of death.
If he does not attain it at the time of death, he attains it when he has become a deva.
If he does not attain it when he has become a deva, then by that passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, he attains paccekabodhi.
In this regard, that which one attains here and now in this very life is penetration (*nibbedha*);
that which one attains in the future as private enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*) is the residual impression (*vāsanā*).
These sixteen discourses stand encompassing the entire teaching.
By these sixteen suttas, the ninefold discourses are analyzed.

And that [analysis] pertains to one who is wise, not to one of poor wisdom; to one who is disciplined, not to one who is undisciplined; to one who dwells without worldly activity. By nature, defilement prevails in the world.
That defilement is threefold:
There is the corruption of craving, the corruption of views, and the corruption of misconduct.
When one arises from that corruption, the corruption becomes established among phenomena; it becomes established among worldly things.
In this regard, for one who is unskilled in view, if he misapprehends both that virtue and that view, then that constitutes his corruption of craving.
But if he thinks, "By means of this virtue, or vow, or holy life, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity," then for one who holds such wrong view, there is the corruption of wrong view.
However, if he is established in virtue, his virtue and vows are unmisapprehended;
for that virtuous person, that which is rightly undertaken produces non-regret all the way up to the knowledge and vision of liberation, and that occurs to him even in this very life.
Whether for one who has passed away, or for one still remaining right there, or through subsequent rebirths in other aggregates—having heard thus:
"Good conduct leads to latent tendencies"—this is called a discourse pertaining to latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

In that regard, for one established in moral discipline, the mind is free from hindrances; the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the sake of abandoning the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) from that state.
Thus one attains the ultimate goal, Nibbāna—whether by attaining ultimate Nibbāna within the interval of a teaching, or by attaining the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) on a single seat.
In this regard, two types of persons attain the noble Dhamma: the follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*) and the follower by Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).
In this context, the follower by Dhamma is one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching, while the follower by faith is one who is led.
Therein, the one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching is of two kinds:
some have sharp faculties, and some have dull faculties.
In that regard, the person to be guided (*neyya*) is also of two kinds:
some have sharp faculties and some have dull faculties.

Among them, the one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*) but has dull faculties, and the one who is to be guided but has sharp faculties—these individuals are of unequal faculties.

In this regard, these individuals with equal faculties fall away from the state of one who understands through a condensed presentation (*ugghaṭitaññū*), while the one who understands through an elaborated presentation (*vipañcitaññū*) and the one who is led (*neyya*) remain on the intermediate ground;
these are the three types of persons.

Therein, the fourth and the fifth—namely, the one who understands through a condensed presentation, the one who understands through an elaborated presentation, and the one who is led—are such that, among them, the one who understands through a condensed presentation [is foremost].
A person, having acquired the faculties and standing on the plane of vision,
attains the fruit of stream-entry and becomes a "single-seed" (ekabījī), the first type of stream-enterer. In that regard,

a person who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū), having acquired the faculties and standing on the plane of vision, attains the fruit of stream-entry and becomes a "family-to-family" (kolaṅkolo) practitioner, the second type of stream-enterer.

In this regard, the person to be guided (neyya-puggala), having acquired the faculties and standing on the plane of vision, attains the fruit of stream-entry and becomes one who has "seven births at most"; this is the third type of stream-enterer.
These three types of persons stand in the fruit of stream-entry due to the diversity of their faculties:

the one who understands through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññū) is a "single-seeder" (ekabījī); the one who understands through an elaborated explanation (vipañcitaññū) is a "family-to-family" (kolaṅkolo); the one who is to be guided is "one who has seven births at most."
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
However, if one exerts oneself further than that, one reaches Nibbāna, the ultimate goal.
In this regard, there are two types of persons who possess keen faculties: the person who gains knowledge through a condensed presentation (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
Having attained the fruit of non-returning, there are those who attain final nibbāna in the interval and those who attain final nibbāna upon landing.
Among them, the person who gains knowledge through exposition is one of keen faculties;
these two types of persons attain the fruit of non-returning as those who attain final nibbāna without exertion and those who attain final nibbāna with exertion.
In this regard, one who is "to-be-led" (neyya) and attains the fruit of non-returning becomes one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Among those who understand through a condensed teaching (ugghaṭitaññū) and those who understand through an elaborated teaching (vipañcitaññū), by the diversity of their faculties, the person who understands through a condensed teaching and possesses sharp faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval;
the person who understands through a condensed teaching and possesses dull faculties becomes one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
There are those who understand through a condensed teaching and those who understand through an elaborated teaching.

Due to the diversity of their faculties, a person who understands through a condensed teaching and possesses sharp faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna with exertion, or one who attains final nibbāna in the interval; whereas a person who understands through a condensed teaching and possesses dull faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna upon landing.

One who gains knowledge through exposition and has sharp faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion; one who gains knowledge through exposition and has dull faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna with exertion;
one who is guidable becomes one who attains final nibbāna upon landing; one who gains knowledge through exposition and has sharp faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion;
one who gains knowledge through exposition and has dull faculties becomes one who attains final nibbāna with exertion; and one who is guidable becomes one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Thus, there are five non-returners, the sixth is the once-returner, and three stream-enterers; these are the nine trainees (*sekkha*).

Among them, when a person who gains knowledge by a condensed summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*) and possesses sharp faculties attains *arahantship*, they become two types of persons: one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) and one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).

Among them, when a person who gains knowledge by a condensed summary and possesses dull faculties attains *arahantship*, they become two types of persons: one who remains for an eon (*ṭhitakappī*) and one of penetrating nature (*paṭivedhanabhāva*).
In this regard, there are two types of persons who reach Arahantship among those of keen faculties who gain knowledge through detailed exposition: one capable of volition and one capable of guarding.

Among them, for the person of dull faculties who gains knowledge through detailed exposition, there are two types upon reaching Arahantship: if he exerts volition, he does not attain final Nibbāna; if he does not exert volition, he attains final Nibbāna.
If he guards [his attainment], he does not attain final Nibbāna; if he does not guard it, he attains final Nibbāna.

In this regard, a person who is guidable (*neyya*), though devoted to the practice of meditation, is subject to decline, or is one whose destiny is fixed by action, or is "equal-headed" (*samasīsi*). These nine types of individuals and this fourfold discourse belong to the category of defilement and the category of those beyond training (*asekkha*).
Within these individuals, the tenfold power of the Tathāgata operates. What is the tenfold power?
Here, when the Wheel of Dhamma has not yet been set in motion by the Blessed Buddhas, sons of the gods of great influence approach with a request, saying:

"May the Sugata teach the Dhamma. Surveying with his unsurpassed Buddha-eye, he sees three groups of beings: those destined for rightness, those destined for wrongness, and those who are undetermined.

Among them, it is impossible that one in the group destined for rightness would fall into wrong mindfulness; it is impossible that he would pass away without a teacher; but it is possible that he would attain meditative absorption.

In that regard, it is impossible for one belonging to the group fixed in falsehood to enter upon the noble practice; however, it is possible for such a person to enter upon the ignoble, false practice.

In that regard, it is possible for one belonging to the undetermined group who practices rightly to go to the group fixed in rightness; however, it is impossible for one who practices wrongly to go to the group fixed in rightness.

"It is possible that one who practices rightly will go to the group of those destined for rightness; it is possible that one who practices wrongly will go to the group of those destined for wrongness.

While I, being a perfectly enlightened Buddha, survey these three [groups] with the unsurpassed Buddha-eye, it is impossible that anyone could rightfully challenge me, saying: 'There are these teachings which you have not fully awakened to.'"
It is impossible that anyone could rightfully challenge you—who claim to be free from lust—on the grounds that your taints (āsava) are not yet exhausted.
Furthermore, it is impossible that this teaching of the Dhamma for this group of the undetermined (aniyata-rāsi) does not lead to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it;
rather, when instructed in such a way, my disciple from the group of the undetermined attains distinction between what was before and what comes after.
"It is impossible that he will not realize it.

It is impossible that the Sage—who, by means of defining the Dhamma, tames the various classes of gods, nāgas, and yakkhas through diverse expressions—will go to the further shore of what is beyond, having spoken from a causal standpoint.
This is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).
But it is impossible that these seven kinds of linguistic expression should not be fully mastered through etymological analysis; such a case does not exist.
This is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
Furthermore, it is impossible that this meaning should not be made known to disciples who delight in thorough understanding through linguistic expression; such a case does not exist.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
High-ranking sons of the gods approached and asked questions.

It is impossible that for one who is afflicted by physical or mental suffering—whether having a withered hand or being lame and slow in foot—the meaning would not be analyzed; such a case does not exist.
The analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
That in whom something exists will not have it cease—that possibility does not exist.
For that which has not ceased for them will not come to cease for them—that possibility does not exist.
Thus, for the cessation of the origin [of suffering], there are the ten unwholesome courses of action.
That a woman should become Māra, or Indra, or Brahmā, or a Tathāgata, or a wheel-turning monarch—that possibility does not exist;
that a man should become a wheel-turning monarch or Sakka, lord of the devas—that possibility does exist.
Such is his power, such is his knowledge; this is called the first Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), which is to be demonstrated.

[It is to be shown] by way of the three groups, the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and the occurrence and cessation of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
It applies to the wholesome and its wholesome results, and to that which pertains to men and women.
This is the first power which the Tathāgata knows thus:
"As for those who belong to the group fixed in rightness, this is not a practice that leads everywhere; rather, this practice leads only to Nibbāna.
In that regard, there may be a group fixed in wrongness; this too is not a practice that leads everywhere."
"Let this be the very path leading to the origin of identity; standing upon this or that practice, one goes to Nibbāna, one goes to the states of deprivation, or one goes among gods and humans.
Whatever practice one might undertake, one would go everywhere—this is the 'everywhere-going' path.
The knowledge regarding this as it truly is, is called the second Tathāgata-power, the knowledge of the everywhere-going path."

Now, this path leading everywhere consists of various inclinations: some are inclined toward sensual pleasures, some toward self-mortification, some toward devotion to the exhaustion of themselves, some believe purification comes through cyclic existence, and some through non-action.

The knowledge by which he understands, as it really is, the diverse inclinations of the world and the various dispositions of beings who are bound by their respective temperaments—this is the third power of the Tathāgata.
Therein, beings are intent upon it; they practice it, develop it, and cultivate it frequently.
For those whose latent tendencies are directed toward that and who are thus intent upon it, that very element carries them along.
But which of these elements—whether the element of renunciation, the element of power, some form of success, or some form of perversion—are they intent upon?
They do not perceive anything further beyond that.
Clinging to that very position regarding aging and death, they declare: "Only this is true; all else is false."
Just as the Blessed One [understood] the speech of Sakka, lord of the devas—
whatever knowledge therein is according to reality—
this is called the fourth power of a Tathāgata.
In that regard, whatever element is supreme, they initiate it through both body and speech;
this initiation is volition, which is mental action (kamma). The Tathāgata understands the distinction between such mental action as follows:
"By this being, possessing such an element, such an action was performed in the past."
“By this cause, such a result ripens for him either now, or it will ripen in the future.
In this way, he understands the present time: “This person, having such a nature, performs this action;
yet because of craving and views, by this cause, its result will not arise in this very life.”
Or else, in another way, he understands thus: "This person will perform such a kind of kamma in the future;

by this cause, such a result will arise for him; by this cause, among the four meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), this meditation subject is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future. ... [and so on] ...

Thus, he understands the diversity of the ripening of undertakings of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of their causes and conditions, and in terms of their high and low, inferior and superior nature; this is called the fifth power of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the ripening of kamma.
Likewise, regarding beings who undertake such undertakings of kamma, he understands therein:
"For this person, who is intent on kamma and of a lustful temperament, the elements of renunciation reach fulfillment; for him, [the factors] following upon lust..."

The first jhāna becomes defiled for one who is conceited; however, if he again exerts further effort and applies himself to the practice conducive to distinction regarding the mind that has reached the purification of jhāna, then for him—
remaining in the first jhāna which is itself conducive to jhāna— the second jhāna reaches purification.
And for one desiring to attain the third jhāna, the faculty of mental joy remains obsessing the mind;
that rapture remains directed toward the third jhāna, which shares its own specific quality.
This is so provided that he understands, as it truly is, the escape from it.

The fourth jhāna of the Tathāgata indeed becomes purified; those states conducive to the decline of the fourth jhāna, and the place where those states arise—by means of these, the fourth jhāna is seen as purified.
Thus, through the attainment according to one's inclination, the four attainments, the three gateways to liberation, and the eight liberations and jhānas constitute the four jhānas as liberations.
There are thus eight liberations and three gateways to liberation.
"Concentration" refers to the four concentrations:
concentration through desire, concentration through energy, concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation.
"Attainments" refers to the four meditative attainments according to one's inclination. Such is the defilement regarding these jhānas and liberative attainments for a person of a lustful temperament.

In this way, for a person of hateful temperament, of deluded temperament, or of lustful temperament, there is such purification; and whatever knowledge there is herein regarding things as they truly are, which is not shared by any beings—this is called the sixth power of a Tathāgata.
In that regard, the Tathāgata understands thus: mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena receive the designation "faculty" when they partake of development.
Taking the stage of sovereignty as their basis, they receive the name "power" (*bala*), because the mind has become firm;
taking that faculty of mind (*manindriya*) as their basis, they receive the name "energy" (*vīriya*), because they have taken up the element of exertion.
Thus, O King, such was his knowledge, and he gave this teaching on the Dhamma: "These persons are endowed with these qualities."

This is the knowledge of the differences in the faculties, powers, and energy of other beings and other individuals—those who are endowed with various dispositions, underlying tendencies, latent biases, and inclinations—considered both in terms of their modes and their variations.
This is called the seventh power of a Tathāgata: the knowledge of the differences in the faculties, powers, and energy of other beings and other individuals.
Furthermore, regarding that [knowledge], the Tathāgata, in relation to the worlds and the stages, as well as the fetters and those in training, [knows] the course [of beings] by means of two powers.

He understands [this]; through the recollection of past lives, he understands the cycle of existence in the past and now in the present, and through the divine eye, he understands passing away and rebirth—thus these two powers are directed from the divine eye.
That which was the range of the divine eye in the past time is now the range of mindfulness; thus, for himself and for others...

And [he possesses] the knowledge of past lives, manifold and of various kinds, and with the divine eye [he perceives] the present time—these are two powers of the Tathāgata: the eighth is the knowledge of past lives, and the ninth is the divine eye.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands the meditative absorptions (jhāna) of noble persons as purification and as conducive to penetration; this is...
"The person, by this path and by this practice, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,
enters upon it, and dwells therein"— thus is the knowledge of the destruction of one's own taints;
and the destruction of the taints of the nine types of Arahants, starting from those who have attained the four stages in this very life, is specific to each case.
For those in training and for arahants without limitation:
therein, the liberation of mind is free from taints by way of two taints—the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence;
the liberation by wisdom is free from taints by way of two taints—the taint of views and the taint of ignorance. Of these two liberations...
Knowledge of things as they truly are—this is called the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata.

Established in these ten powers, the Tathāgata teaches the fivefold teaching: that which pertains to defilement, that which pertains to purification, that which pertains to vision, that which pertains to development, and that which pertains to the state of one beyond training.
In this regard, non-greed is the escape from the corruption of craving;
non-delusion is the escape from the corruption of views;
and the three wholesome states are the escape from the corruption of misconduct.
What is the cause?
These three types of mental misconduct:
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
Therein, covetousness establishes bodily action as mental misconduct; it establishes taking what is not given and all verbal action connected therewith;
and it establishes false speech, all untruth, all silence, and all slander and spite. Covetousness is an unwholesome root.
In the case of good conduct, [there is] good conduct [as the opposite of] false speech, taking what is not given, and covetousness.
Volition: therein, ill will establishes bodily action as mental misconduct;
all that—drawing near, drawing further, binding, and delighting—establishes vocal action as such;
and covetousness, ill will, and wrong view set in motion mental misconduct, namely, divisive speech, harsh speech, and wrong view.
Whatever wrong view, whether born of greed or born of hatred, that person possesses— since it has arisen entirely from wrong view—
it is for this reason that they establish wrong view, establish the verbal action of sexual misconduct, and establish idle chatter.
These three types of misconduct are the roots of unwholesomeness.
Covetousness is greed;
ill will is hatred;
wrong view is delusion.
These establish the eight wrongnesses.

When those three unwholesome roots are grasped, the tenfold unwholesome root reaches its full completion. And the escape from that threefold corruption of misconduct is the discourse dealing with the residual impressions (*vāsanā*).
In this regard, there is an extensive exposition such as greed, hatred, and delusion; therein, because greed is predominant, for that reason greed is designated among those states.

In this context, this delusion is unwholesome delusion; this is ignorance (*avijjā*). It is fourfold, being attached to form (*rūpa*): one regards form as self, or, being possessed by ignorance, regards the self as possessing form, or form as being in the self, or the self as being in form.

In this regard, what is the position that speaks of the annihilation of personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)? It is the view that "the soul is the same as the body," the nihilistic view (*natthikadiṭṭhi*), the fortuitous-origination view (*adhiccasamuppannadiṭṭhi*), and the view that one person acts and another experiences [the result].
Of the sixty subsequent aeons, three terms pertain to eternalism within the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*):

"the soul is one thing, the body another," as well as non-action (*akiriyavāda*). One who desires suffering falls into causelessness (*ahetuka*), and there is the non-appropriation of kamma, and he honored everything.
In this regard, the Ājīvakas proclaim eighty-six ways of purification through the cycle of existence, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is vain.
Just as personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) has four bases, so too, with respect to the five aggregates, personality-view has twenty bases and thus partakes of eternalism.

Other Ājīvakas and Eternalists partake of and misapprehend virtue and observance (*sīlabbata*), thinking: "By means of this, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity"—this is the misapprehension of virtue and observance.

In this regard, one who stands among those characterized by the influence of latent tendencies views form as self, and is perplexed, doubtful, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the view that "the soul and the body are identical," concerning the past, the future, or both the past and the future...
This is the defilement for one standing among those characterized by latent tendencies.

In this context, one abandons all doubt through the faculty of faith, perceives arising and passing away through the faculty of wisdom, unifies the mind through the faculty of concentration, and exerts effort through the faculty of energy.
Thus, by means of these five faculties, the follower by faith (saddhānusārī), delighting in verified confidence (aveccappasāda), arouses immediate concentration (anantariya-samādhi).
With the faculties purified, the follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) arouses immediate concentration through the absence of conditions.
He understands, as it really is: "This is suffering."
This discourse on the Truths pertains to the section on vision.
Of the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), three fetters are to be abandoned by vision and have been entirely abandoned; these two [remaining ones] are produced by persons.
Therein, the three unwholesome roots (*akusala-mūla*)—which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—are cast off and produce rebirth in the six realms of existence.
Therein, when covetousness and ill will have been attenuated, six states reach the limit of exhaustion, while two states remain.
For him, covetousness and ill will are completely and utterly exhausted;
one state remains.
And he produces it by way of the conceit "I am.

Although there are four other defilements here—namely, lust for form, lust for existence, ignorance, and restlessness—which, being of the nature of the conceit "I am," are not capable of overturning that conceit, he nevertheless undertakes the abandonment of all of them through the abandonment of the conceit "I am.

When these are exhausted, this is the stage of higher vision among the five persons in training and the three who have entered the path and the two who stand in the fruit; it is the discourse pertaining to the development of cultivation.
Beyond that is the discourse pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkha*). In some places, the ground is pressed down.
This is the fifth discourse.

It was taught for three types of persons—the worldling (*puthujjana*), the one in training (*sekkha*), and the one beyond training—and it pertains to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*) and to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
The portion pertaining to vision belongs to the worldling;
the portion pertaining to cultivation belongs to the five types of trainees;
that which was first described as the portion pertaining to those beyond training belongs to all Arahants.
That [investigation], moreover, is fivefold and should be sought in twenty-seven aspects.
Beyond those, its destinies are further [expanded].
And yet, in brief, it falls into fifty aspects; those fifty aspects taught in the Dispensation, when condensed, fall into ten aspects.
Those [passages] that stand as a presentation of the Noble Truths fall, by way of summary, into eight modes.
And those that constitute the ground for the convergence of the modes within the four common suttas, when summarized, fall into five suttas:
those dealing with defilement, those dealing with purification, those dealing with development, those dealing with penetration, and those dealing with the state of one beyond training.
When these are condensed, they fall into four discourses:

those dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*), those dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), those dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and those dealing with the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).

When these are further condensed, they fall into three discourses: those dealing with worldlings (*puthujjanabhāgiya*), those dealing with trainees (*sekkhabhāgiya*), and those dealing with the state beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
When these are condensed, they fall into two types of discourses (*sutta*): those pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) and those pertaining to prior practice (*pubbayogabhāgiya*).
As it was said by the Blessed One: "The Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, teach the Dhamma seeing two purposes:

[thinking] 'Those endowed with prior practice will master [the teachings] with little difficulty,' and [thinking] 'There will be those who possess prior practice, serving as a support for those who are still striving.'"
In this regard, one who observes the diversity of wisdom within oneself should apply [this method] wherever possible among the eightfold summary of the Suttas.
Having applied it in each respective place, the meaning of the Sutta should be demonstrated.
For it is not possible for anyone to demonstrate the meaning of a Sutta as it truly is, unless they maintain mindfulness, feeling, and mind.
In this regard, these are the summary verses for the preceding discourses:
Blinded by lust, covered by a net,
and the five hindrances.

And that which concerns the purpose of virtue;
and for whom the mind is like a rock—

“Whether openly or in secret.

In this context, what is the fruit?
"The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives according to the Dhamma."
Just as a large umbrella [protects] during the rainy season;
such is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to an evil destination.
This is the fruit.
In this regard, what is the means?
"All phenomena are non-self."
When one sees with wisdom,

“Monk, one endowed with seven factors could even shake the Himalayas, the king of mountains; what need is there to mention the wretched ignorance among the seven [factors]? This is the explanation that should be given.

If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,

Whether openly or in secret:

Established in virtue, two things are to be developed: the development of the mind and the development of wisdom; and the instruction, which is the fruit—the fading away of lust.
In this context, what is the fruit and what is the means?
“A wise person, established in virtue...”
Cultivating the mind and wisdom,
the ardent and discerning bhikkhu shall unravel this tangle.
The first half-verse concerns the means (*upāya*); the latter half-verse concerns the fruit (*phala*).
In the *Nandiyasakka-sutta*, from the beginning up to the six qualities, there is the case of a woman who had lived as a seer (*isi*) and was fond of solitude.
Beyond that, regarding the five qualities, the application of a request (*yācayoga*) must be performed; this is the means.
"For one who has not yet attained [the goal], the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire.
This applies to all six, three, and two.
This is both the means and the fruit.
In this context, what is the command, the fruit, and the means?
“O Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty.”
“Having uprooted the view of self,
one may thus be a crosser over death.

“Always mindful” is the means.
“Having uprooted the view of self, one may thus be a crosser over death” is the fruit.

In this regard, what is the danger?

This is the danger.
In the *Pasenadi-saṃyutta*, in the discourse on the simile of the mountain,

“They are not worth a sixteenth part of it.

whatever has been attained and whatever is yet to be attained—
They always rejoice and they always grieve—
whatever beings have been,
and whatever teachers shall appear.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world,
and the well-taught factors of enlightenment—
the Eightfold Path is the best among paths.
And the three supreme attainments:
Restraint in body is good,
and what is to be done has been taught.
There is no love equal to that for oneself;
the Noble Ones have taught three [ways].
Delighting in what is wholesome with the body,
The discipline and sensual pleasure in the world;
the factors of enlightenment well-taught;
and that which is difficult to see, the unshakable, and the further and the beyond.
In the *Peṭakopadesa*, the second chapter, titled "The Foundation of the Dispensation," is completed.
